name: Aisha Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Aisha. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Partline Distribution, which supplies car parts to about three hundred independent garages. Brake pads, oil filters, batteries, wiper blades, the boring parts that keep cars on the road. I spend my day in the stock system, checking what's running low, ordering from about fifteen manufacturers and arguing about delivery dates.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I know the catalogue better than anyone. A garage rings about a 2014 diesel and I know which filter fits without looking. What wears me down is the system changes, they've changed our ordering screens three times in five years, and every time I'm the last one to get used to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, sensible, let's get on with work. I'm not one for big opinions online, I'd probably just say it at lunch with Steve from the warehouse. Most people at work would shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be a weight off. I've never used these AI things and I don't really want to start. If they stay as a little helper somewhere in the system, I can carry on the way I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. Same suppliers, same stock system, same checks every morning at eight. We'd keep the savings ticking over and maybe finally replace the old family car next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal life, which is what I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want to start using AI. What puts you off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust what I can't check. If I order four hundred brake pads, I want to know why it's four hundred. I've seen what happens when a system gets it wrong. Last winter the old forecast program at our parts warehouse ordered summer tyres in November.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the managers would keep talking about AI anyway, because it sounds modern. Mr Holt, my boss, loves a new word. But if it doesn't change anything, it's just talk, and I can live with talk.

S0.say: I'd say good, sensible, let's get on with work, probably just at lunch with Steve from the warehouse. I don't share big opinions online.
S0.think: It'd be a weight off, because I've never used AI and don't want to start. If it stays a little helper inside the system, I carry on the way I know.
S0.do: Carries on with the same suppliers, stock system and eight o'clock checks. Keeps the savings ticking over and plans to replace the old family car next year.
S0.feel: Calm, glad that normal life carries on.
S0.quote: Last winter the old forecast program at our parts warehouse ordered summer tyres in November.
S0.fieldNote: Aisha's pride is her catalogue knowledge: she knows parts without looking. Her distrust of AI is about not being able to check its reasoning, backed by a real story of a bad forecast. She wants normal life and says so plainly.

steps.text: Keep the eight o'clock stock checks and the same suppliers
Replace the old family car next year as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the way of the world, every job changes. At work I'd say I'll learn whatever they need me to learn, because you have to say that. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried. Ordering parts is exactly what these programs are built for, and I'm the slowest in the team with new systems. If Partline cuts from five buyers to three, I'm afraid they'd look at me first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the company's training if they put me on it, but I wouldn't go looking for it. At home I'd stop the car plan and keep the money, because we've only got about three months saved. I'd also make sure Mr Holt knows how many garages ask for me by name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A knot in the stomach on Monday mornings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd do training only if they put you on it. Why wait to be asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't want to waste evenings learning something that might change again next year. I've done that three times with the ordering screens. I know it's a risk, Imran tells me I'm being stubborn, and he's probably right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is Imran, and how does his work fit in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Imran's my husband, he's a mechanic at the Toyota dealership. The funny thing? My husband will be fine as a mechanic, because computers don't change brake pads. If things go bad for me, his wage keeps the lights on, though not the mortgage on its own.

S1.say: I'd say every job changes and it's the way of the world, and tell work I'll learn whatever they need. I wouldn't post anything.
S1.think: Ordering parts is exactly what these programs do, and I'm the slowest with new systems. If Partline cuts from five buyers to three, I'm afraid they'd look at me first.
S1.do: Does the company AI training only if assigned, not by choice. Cancels the car replacement to keep about three months of savings, and makes sure her boss knows how many garages ask for her by name.
S1.feel: Anxious, with a knot in her stomach on Monday mornings.
S1.quote: My husband will be fine as a mechanic, because computers don't change brake pads.
S1.fieldNote: Aisha's public line is cooperative, but privately she expects to be first in line for cuts. Her resistance is partly fatigue from repeated system changes. Her husband's hands-on job is her household's quiet safety net, and she knows it doesn't cover the mortgage alone.

steps.text: Hold off replacing the family car and keep the cash
Wait to see if Partline assigns AI training before learning it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody in charge should have seen it coming. At work I'd keep my head down and do my job well. I'm not the type to march, but I'd vote for whoever seemed to have a sensible plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone within a year of 2028. A program that can think like a person can order brake pads better than me, faster and without lunch breaks. What I keep thinking is that the warehouse lads and Imran have three more years than me, because the robots come later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Steve about a job on the trade counter or the warehouse floor, picking and packing, because I know every part number and robots aren't coming for that until 2031. We'd cut back hard: no holiday, cheaper food shop, cancel the streaming and the kids' tutoring except Sara's maths. And I'd talk to my parents about whether they could help with the mortgage for a while if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The warehouse is a pay cut and physical work. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate the cold in winter, and the pay is maybe two thirds of mine. But a wage is a wage. I know where every part lives in our warehouse, and a picking job at two thirds of my pay would buy us three years to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughter Sara?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sara's fifteen and thinks she wants to do accounting. I'd tell her to think again, gently, because accounting is the same kind of work as mine. Maybe something where you fix things or look after people, like her dad.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and someone in charge should have seen it coming. At work I'd keep my head down, and I'd vote for whoever had a sensible plan.
S2.think: My job is gone within a year of 2028, because a thinking program can order brake pads better than me. The warehouse workers and my husband get three more years than me before robots come.
S2.do: Asks the warehouse supervisor, Steve, for a trade counter or picking job to last until robots arrive around 2031. Cuts the holiday, food bill, streaming and tutoring except her daughter's maths, and asks her parents about help with the mortgage.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake doing the sums.
S2.quote: I know where every part lives in our warehouse, and a picking job at two thirds of my pay would buy us three years to think.
S2.fieldNote: For Aisha the robot lag is concrete: it's the warehouse she walks past every day. Her plan is to step down into hands-on work she knows, accepting less pay. Her advice to her daughter shows she sees accounting as the same kind of exposed work as her own.

steps.text: Ask Steve for a trade counter or warehouse picking job
Cancel the holiday, streaming and most of the tutoring
Ask her parents about help with the mortgage if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so the government and companies had better plan. At work I'd say I'm willing to move to wherever there's work. I'd still keep it off the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same ending but with a run-up. My job lasts until 2031, maybe a bit after. I'm honestly not sure I'd use the five years well, because I tend to wait until I'm pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more money aside, maybe a hundred and fifty a month extra, to get us from three months to six. I'd keep doing my job and wait a couple of years to see whether it's really happening. If it is, around 2029 I'd ask about moving to the trade counter, where you talk to mechanics face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can breathe. It's a worry I'd put in a drawer and take out now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you tend to wait until you're pushed. Does that worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I know the sensible thing is to start now. But I've seen so many big announcements that came to nothing, and I don't want to throw away a decent job for a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope the company does in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tell us straight. Companies should sit us down and say which jobs go and when, not send an email saying exciting times ahead. If Mr Holt did that, I'd plan properly.

S3.say: I'd say we've been warned, so government and companies had better plan, and tell work I'm willing to move wherever there's work. I'd keep it off the internet.
S3.think: It's the same ending with a run-up, and my job lasts until about 2031. I'm not sure I'd use the five years well, because I wait until I'm pushed.
S3.do: Saves an extra hundred and fifty a month to grow savings from three to six months. Keeps her job and waits a couple of years, then asks about the trade counter around 2029 if the change is clearly coming.
S3.feel: Anxious but able to breathe, a worry kept in a drawer and taken out now and then.
S3.quote: Companies should sit us down and say which jobs go and when, not send an email saying exciting times ahead.
S3.fieldNote: Aisha is unusually honest about her own tendency to wait, even when she knows starting early would be wiser. Past hype makes her sceptical of acting on a forecast. What she wants most is a straight answer from her employer.

steps.text: Save an extra hundred and fifty a month towards six months
Wait until about 2029 before asking about the trade counter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can happen. At work I'd say we should plan, but not panic. I'd probably make a joke that I'll be retired by then, though I won't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 53 when it comes, and the mortgage would have about seven years left. My job would carry on as normal for a long while, and Imran's even longer. I'd be uneasy, but it wouldn't stop me sleeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for the first few years I'd mostly wait and see, and keep doing my job well. I'd overpay the mortgage when we can, maybe a hundred a month. If by 2032 it looks real, that's when I'd move to the counter or the warehouse side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in the background. A cloud on the horizon, not rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd joke about being retired. What's behind that joke?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wishful thinking, I suppose. Part of me hopes I can keep my head down until AI sorts itself out, and part of me knows that's how people end up surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you ever try the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if everyone else in the team is using them and they've stopped changing every year. I'd let the younger ones go first and ask them to show me. I'm not proud, I'm just slow.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and we should plan but not panic. I'd joke that I'll be retired by then, though I won't be.
S4.think: I'd be 53, with about seven years left on the mortgage, and both my job and my husband's would last a long while. I'd be uneasy but still sleep.
S4.do: Mostly waits and sees for the first few years while doing her job well. Overpays the mortgage by about a hundred a month, and plans to move to the counter or warehouse around 2032 if the change looks real.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background, like a cloud on the horizon rather than rain.
S4.quote: Part of me hopes I can keep my head down until AI sorts itself out, and part of me knows that's how people end up surprised.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Aisha's resistance shows as patient waiting rather than fear. She is self-aware: her joke about retiring hides a hope that it passes her by. She would follow younger colleagues onto AI tools only once they've settled.

steps.text: Overpay the mortgage by about a hundred a month
Keep buying as normal and reassess around 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't enough for someone like me who's slow to change, and the mortgage doesn't care how fast the world moves. What would help is being told early and honestly, and a guaranteed move to another job in the same company, even a lower one, rather than a redundancy letter.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be the slow one. Everyone talks about learning new skills like it's easy. For some of us, every new screen at work feels like starting school again at 43.

headlineQuote: For some of us, every new screen at work feels like starting school again at 43.
portrait: Aisha Khan, 43, buys car parts for Partline Distribution, which supplies independent garages, and knows the catalogue better than anyone. She has never used AI and is tired of system changes, so she is calm only if AI stalls and anxious under steady change. AGI by 2028 alarms her, and she would step down to the warehouse or trade counter to use the three years before robots arrive. With more warning she admits she would wait to be pushed, saving a little and watching. Her husband's mechanic job is the household's safety net, and what she wants most is honesty and a guaranteed place in the company.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years isn't enough for someone slow to change and the mortgage doesn't wait.
whatWouldHelp: Being told early and honestly, and a guaranteed move to another job in the same company, even a lower one, instead of a redundancy letter.
